lessons.title: What Theatre Is and What It Does
lessons.content:
Theatre is a live art in which performers present a story or a situation to an audience in a shared space at a shared time. It differs from film and television in three decisive ways: it is live, so nothing can be re-taken and the audience's presence changes the performance; it is a collective art, made by writer, director, actors, designers, technicians and front-of-house staff together; and it is ephemeral, existing only in the moment of performance, which is why the record of it - script, notes, photographs, reviews, recollections - is so important. Its basic elements are the performer, the audience, the space, the text or scenario, and the design and technical support that frame the action.

Theatre's roots lie in ritual, ceremony and celebration. Long before purpose-built playhouses there were religious festivals, harvest ceremonies, masquerade and procession, storytelling and song; the dramas of ancient Greece grew out of festivals of Dionysus, medieval European theatre out of the church, and in the Caribbean the oldest performance traditions are indigenous ceremony, African-derived masquerade and ritual, and the folk festivals that survive today - Junkanoo, Carnival, Jonkonnu, Hosay, Maypole, Quadrille, Christmas sports and night-time masquerade. Theatre in the region is therefore both an inherited art form and a continuation of community performance, and the two have always fed each other.

Theatre's functions overlap and shift with context. It entertains by holding attention with story, suspense, comedy, spectacle, music and dance; it educates and informs, dramatising history, health, civics and social issues; it persuades and advocates, as in campaigning theatre and forum theatre; it celebrates and commemorates in national and religious events; it explores and preserves culture and language, including the region's dialects and creoles; it creates community by bringing people into a shared room; and it provides work and enterprise for thousands in the creative industries. When you watch or make a performance, the useful questions are what it is trying to do, for whom, and how well the staging choices serve that aim. The same questions are the basis of criticism, and the same skills of observation are the basis of practice.
objectives: Define theatre and distinguish it from recorded media
Outline the origins of theatre in ritual and festival, including Caribbean forms
Explain the functions of theatre and analyse a performance's intention and effect

experiment.description: Stage Basics: Match each element of a performance to what it does for the audience.

lessons.title: The Theatre Company and its Roles
lessons.content:
No performance is the work of one person. A theatre company is a temporary or permanent organisation in which each role carries a distinct responsibility, and understanding those roles is what makes it possible to work effectively in a production. The playwright creates the script - the story, structure, characters, dialogue and stage directions; in devised theatre the script is made collaboratively by the whole company. The producer is responsible for the business side: raising and managing money, setting the budget, arranging contracts and rights, booking the venue, marketing and ensuring the production completes on schedule; the producer may be a company, a school department or a single entrepreneur. The director interprets the script, establishes the concept and style, casts the actors, guides rehearsals, integrates the design elements and holds the overall vision; assistant and stage directors support that work and rehearse scenes, and in educational productions the teacher often also directs.

The actors create the performances: they analyse the script, develop character, learn lines and blocking, work with voice, movement and emotional truth, and maintain consistency across a run. Around them the production team builds the world of the play. The set designer produces the ground plan, elevations and model, and the scenographic concept; the costume designer researches, designs and oversees making, fitting and maintenance of costume; the lighting designer plans the plot, instruments, colour and cue sheet; the sound designer prepares effects, music and reinforcement; a properties maker or props master prepares hand props and furniture; the make-up and hair team designs and applies looks, including fantasy, period and mask work. The technical director and technicians install and run the equipment, and the production manager coordinates schedules, budgets and safety.

During the run, the stage manager holds everything together: keeping the prompt book with cues, running rehearsals and calling every cue in performance, managing the backstage and the entrances, keeping the rehearsal and performance reports, and liaising with front of house. Front-of-house staff sell and check tickets, seat the audience, run the bar or refreshments and manage the auditorium; the house manager is responsible for audience safety and comfort. Beyond the immediate company are the publicist and marketing team, the box office, the photographer, the graphic designer who makes the poster and programme, the van driver and the person who feeds everyone on a long technical rehearsal. Roles overlap in small companies - the same person may design the lights and operate them - but the responsibilities never disappear, and production meetings exist to make sure that each one is owned by somebody. In a school production, the most common cause of a weak show is not a lack of talent or equipment but an unassigned responsibility.
objectives: Identify the roles in a theatre company and describe each responsibility
Explain how a production is organised from script to performance
Allocate production responsibilities and describe how the team communicates

experiment.description: Role Assign: Take a production brief and assign every responsibility, then find the gaps that would stall the show.

lessons.title: Performance Spaces and Staging Forms
lessons.content:
The space shapes what can be performed and how the audience experiences it. In a proscenium arch theatre, the audience faces the stage through a framed opening; the fourth wall is intact, illusion and spectacle are easy to create, sight lines and flying scenery are manageable, but the relationship between actor and audience is relatively distant. A thrust stage projects into the auditorium with the audience on three sides: the audience is closer and more involved, entrances can come from the vomitoria or aisles, but scenery must be low and sight lines from the sides must be checked. An arena or theatre-in-the-round surrounds the acting area with audience on all four sides: intimacy and energy are high and elaborate scenery is impossible, so the space must be defined by lighting, props and the actors themselves. A black box is a flexible room in which seating and staging can be rearranged for each production, from end-on to traverse to promenade. Found, street and site-specific performance takes place in markets, courtyards, churches, beaches, buses and public squares, where the audience may come and go and where the venue itself carries meaning - the form used by much Caribbean community, carnival and touring theatre.

Alongside the space, stagings are classified as representational, where the audience watches a world presented as if they were not there, and presentational, where performers acknowledge and address the audience directly - narration, song, aside, chorus and direct address. Folk and popular Caribbean forms such as carnival, Junkanoo, ring games, storytelling and the traditional Christmas sports are overwhelmingly presentational: they invite participation, are performed in the round or in procession, and are designed to involve rather than to conceal. Contemporary directors often mix the two, using direct address to break the realism and involving the audience in the action.

Practical constraints decide as much as artistic preference. Access to power, lighting positions and hanging points, the height of the ceiling, the floor (sprung, raked, sandy, sloping), the availability of wings, dressing rooms, storage and toilet facilities, the number of seats, noise and traffic outside, the weather, and above all safety - fire exits, audience capacity, trip hazards, electrical loading, barriers for crowd control - all shape the planning. A promenade performance through a town needs marshals, a portable sound system and a rehearsal of the route; a school hall may be the only space available and requires imagination plus masking. The right answer is always: use the space as a co-creator, plan for its limits, and never let spectacle outrun safety.
objectives: Compare proscenium, thrust, arena, black box and found spaces and their demands
Distinguish representational from presentational staging and give Caribbean examples
Assess a venue's practical constraints, including safety, and plan a staging for it

experiment.description: Space Planner: Place a scene in three different stage configurations and compare the sight lines and effects.

lessons.title: Voice and Speech for the Stage
lessons.content:
The actor's voice is an instrument that must be trained, warmed and protected. Everything begins with breath: diaphragmatic or intercostal breathing, in which the air is drawn low into the body so that the shoulders stay still and the abdomen moves, gives the support and control needed to fill a space without shouting. Actors warm up before every performance - gentle stretching, freeing the neck and jaw, humming, lip trills, tongue twisters, resonant vowel work and range exercises - and they protect the voice by drinking water, avoiding prolonged shouting and smoky or air-conditioned extremes, and resting the voice when ill. Projection is not volume but carrying power: it uses supported breath, open resonating spaces (chest, mouth, mask of the face, nose, sinuses), forward placement and the intention to be heard at the back of the house, and it can be amplified by using the space and turning to the audience rather than by straining the throat. Pitch, pace, pause and volume are the actor's dynamics: pitch rises with excitement and falls with gravity, pace changes with the character's thought and urgency, pause is the most powerful of all and gives weight to the words around it, and volume distinguishes a confidence from a secret.

Articulation and pronunciation make meaning audible. Articulation uses the lips, tongue, teeth, soft palate and jaw to form consonants clearly without becoming clipped or over-precise; poor articulation produces the mumbling that destroys a good performance. Pronunciation is the way a word is said, and actors must be consistent within a production and respect the text - a script's spellings or apostrophes may signal a particular pronunciation, rhythm or dialect. Diction exercises, reading aloud, tongue twisters and recording one's own voice build accuracy. English as spoken in the Caribbean is rich in varieties: the standard and formal registers used in presentation, the regional accents of Jamaica, Trinidad, Guyana, Barbados and the other territories, the creoles and patois that carry everyday life, and the traditional dialects of rural communities. Each carries meaning, history and identity, and actors must be able to move between them without shame and without caricature. A character's class, region, education and origin are audible in speech, and dialect work is done by listening to speakers, studying recordings, learning the vowel and consonant patterns and, where possible, working with a voice or dialect coach.

Choral speaking, storytelling and verse demand a further set of skills. In choral speaking a group synchronises the voice, deciding on unison passages, solo lines, antiphonal exchanges, dynamics, rhythm, pace and pause, so that the group speaks as one instrument - a form that suits folk poetry, protest verse and traditional storytelling. Verse speaking requires attention to metre, rhyme and breath so that the line lives without becoming sing-song. In song, the actor must sing in character, matching pitch, diction and emotional intention, and blend with an ensemble rather than perform in isolation. Throughout, the standard is truth: the audience must hear not a voice being displayed but a person who means what they are saying.
objectives: Use breathing, projection and resonance to be heard in a space without straining
Apply articulation, pronunciation, pitch, pace, pause and volume to a text
Work in dialect, verse and choral speaking truthfully and without caricature

experiment.description: Voice Studio: Work through a line using breath, projection, pause and pace and compare the effect of each choice.

lessons.title: Movement, Mime and Physical Theatre
lessons.content:
An actor performs with the whole body, and the body must be trained, warm and expressive. A warm-up prepares the instrument: joint mobilising from head to ankles, stretches, spine rolls, isolations of head, shoulders, ribs and hips, balance and alignment work, and a check of posture, since a body that stands badly cannot lie, sit or walk well on stage. Alignment means the head over the shoulders, the shoulders over the hips and the weight over the feet, giving the ease from which all movement begins; tension must be released, because the audience reads tension even when the actor feels it internally. Actors learn to move in character rather than as themselves: how a person stands, walks, sits, gestures and occupies space reveals age, class, health, occupation, confidence and attitude far more tellingly than words alone. Stage movement is also stagecraft: crossing with purpose, sharing the stage without masking other actors or the audience's view, upstaging, cheating out to make a gesture visible, handling props securely, and moving on cue rather than wandering.

Mime and physical theatre place the story in the body. A mime artist creates objects, spaces and forces that do not exist - walls, doors, weights, ropes, weather - with precise isolation, resistance, consistent weight and clear shape, obeying the rules of the imagined world so rigidly that the audience sees what is not there. Techniques include isolation of body parts, opposition and counterbalance, articulating the fixed point against which movement works, using the eyes to lead, and telling the action with clear beginnings, middles and ends. Physical theatre extends this into storytelling in which objects, chairs, bodies, masks, stilts, cloth and human pyramids become the vocabulary - the tradition seen in Caribbean street performance, carnival characters (Midnight Robber, Pierrot Grenade, Moko Jumbie and Jab Jab), mask work and contemporary ensemble companies. Improvisation sustains it: given circumstances, objectives, obstacles and characters are played out without a script, developing spontaneity, listening, acceptance of offers, status awareness and truthful reaction.

Fight and movement safety must be treated as a technical discipline. Stage combat - slaps, punches, kicks, chokes, falls, swordplay or knife work - is choreographed in exact counts and rehearsed slowly, with distance, timing, eye contact, a safe target and a believable reaction, and it is cut to the audience's sight lines so that nothing is exposed. Performers never improvise violence, never work tired on a fight call, always rehearse at reduced speed before full pace, and know a safety call that stops the action immediately. Falls and throws need mats, rehearsal and correct technique; lifts need trained strength, spotting and agreement; and stunts, fire, weapons, heights and water require specialist supervision and a risk assessment. Nothing on stage is worth a broken bone, and the safest-looking fight is the one that has been rehearsed most.
objectives: Warm up and align the body and move expressively in character
Create believable mime and physical theatre, using the body to tell a story
Choreograph and rehearse movement and staged violence safely

experiment.description: Movement Lab: Create a mimed task with a real weight and check whether the imagined object stays consistent.

lessons.title: Characterisation and Rehearsal Practice
lessons.content:
Characterisation begins with the text. The actor reads the script repeatedly to establish what the character says and does, what others say about them, what the stage directions reveal and what the historical, social and cultural circumstances imply. From this reading come the character's given circumstances: time, place, relationships, past, social position, health, age and immediate situation. The actor then establishes a through-line of objectives - what the character wants in the play, in the scene and in each beat of the scene - and the obstacles, internal and external, that stand in the way. Subtext is what is really meant beneath the words, and the actor plays it: two people agreeing politely on the surface while fighting under it is the commonest form of dramatic interest. A useful discipline is to ask of each line what the character is doing with it (warning, pleading, boasting, testing, concealing) rather than how it should sound; doing produces the sound, and playing an emotion directly usually produces cliche.

The physical and vocal work follows: how this person stands, sits, walks and gestures, their tempo and rhythm, their accent and vocabulary, their habits and mannerisms, their relationship to space and to objects. Actors build this from observation of real people, photographs, recordings, interviews and imagination, and they keep a notebook of such observations. Emotion must be both felt and controlled: an actor who genuinely weeps may be unable to speak, while an actor who fakes it is not believed. The solution is emotional memory used with care, an active imagination, an understanding of the circumstances, and technique that keeps the performance repeatable - because it must be produced again tomorrow, whether or not the actor feels it today. Acting styles vary: naturalistic work demands invisible technique, verse and classical work demands rhythm and rhetorical shape, comedy demands timing and truth within exaggeration, and mask, musical and physical forms demand external skill as much as inner life.

Rehearsal is a disciplined process with stages. In the read-and-discuss stage the company reads the script and the director establishes the concept; in blocking, moves and positions are set and recorded; in working rehearsals scenes are explored, character developed, lines learned and business built; in run-throughs the act or the play is played continuously to find pace and continuity; and in technical and dress rehearsals the work is integrated with lights, sound, costume and props. The actor's contribution to that process is professional: arriving early, warmed up and off book; learning lines properly and picking up cues promptly; taking direction and notes without argument and applying them the next time; keeping line, blocking and cue records in the script in pencil; being ready when called and quiet when not; supporting rather than competing with fellow actors; contributing ideas at the right moment and committing to the director's decision afterwards; and treating every person in the company, including the newest crew member, with respect. In a production, discipline is not the opposite of creativity - it is what makes creativity usable.
objectives: Analyse a script to establish given circumstances, objectives, obstacles and subtext
Build a character vocally and physically and sustain it through a run
Follow the stages and professional discipline of rehearsal

experiment.description: Character Build: Assemble a character from the text evidence and choose what each line is doing.

lessons.title: Dramatic Structure, Genre and Style
lessons.content:
A play is built from structure. The plot is the sequence of events and, more importantly, the causal chain in which one action causes the next; a story is only a chronicle, while a plot is shaped by conflict. Conflict is the engine of drama and takes several forms: between people, between a person and society, between a person and nature or fate, and within a person. Exposition supplies the information the audience needs to understand the situation - who, where, when, what has happened before - and is best delivered through action and conflict rather than announcement; the inciting incident upsets the balance and sets the story in motion; rising action complicates the situation through obstacles and reversals; the climax is the point of highest tension where the central conflict is engaged decisively; falling action resolves the consequences; and the denouement or resolution settles the world, whether in reconciliation, destruction, or an unsettling question. Subplots mirror, comment on or complicate the main plot, and the theme is the underlying idea the play explores, revealed through the whole action rather than stated by a character.

Character is created through action, dialogue, relationships, contrast and what others say, and characters are drawn as rounded (complex, contradictory, changing) or flat (simple, consistent, functional). A protagonist carries the central conflict, an antagonist opposes, a foil contrasts by similarity, and the chorus, narrator or messenger can comment, inform and shift the audience's perspective. Dialogue does more than convey information: it reveals character and status, drives conflict, creates rhythm, subtext and imagery, and often distinguishes characters by register, dialect, vocabulary, sentence length and interruption. Stage directions and the physical life of the play - entrances, exits, props, music, silence, lighting - carry meaning that the words do not, and much of the actor's and designer's work lies in what the script leaves unsaid.

Genre and style set the audience's expectations and the production's rules. Tragedy traces the fall of a person of consequence through error, fate or flaw, and leaves the audience with pity, fear and insight; comedy exposes human folly through wit, incongruity, misunderstanding and the correction of a social fault, and ends with reconciliation or the restoration of order; farce piles on absurd situation, mistaken identity and physical comedy at high speed; melodrama sets clear virtue against clear villainy with heightened emotion; the musical integrates song, dance and book into a single dramatic structure; tragicomedy mixes registers; and documentary, epic, absurdist, expressionist, Brechtian, forum and site-specific forms each propose a different relationship between stage and audience. In the Caribbean, distinctive forms include folk and dialect drama, pantomime (Jamaica's annual traditional pantomime, which is a musical comedy of local life rather than the British counterpart), carnival and calypso theatre, dub and performance poetry theatre, community and popular theatre, and the post-independence verse and historical plays of writers from Walcott to the present. Style must be consistent and chosen: whether the production is naturalistic, stylised, masked, physical, presentational or mixed determines how everything else - acting, design, sound, tempo - is handled.
objectives: Explain plot, conflict, exposition, climax and resolution in a play
Analyse character and dialogue and distinguish rounded from flat characters
Identify genre and style, including distinctive Caribbean forms, and their effect on production

experiment.description: Structure Map: Break a chosen play into its structural beats and mark the climax and turning points.

lessons.title: Script Analysis and Interpretation
lessons.content:
Script analysis is the disciplined reading of a play so that production decisions rest on evidence rather than guesswork - the work the director, designers and actors all do before rehearsals begin. The first reading establishes the story and the effect; subsequent readings gather evidence about the given circumstances: who these people are, their age, class, work, health and relationships, where and when the play is set, what has happened before the play opens, and what the world outside the room is like. Facts stated in the text are separated from inferences: an actor or director may and should invent what the script does not say, but the invention must not contradict the text, and the difference between fact and choice should be known. Research fills the gaps - the historical period, the social conditions, the real geography, the money, the law, the technology of the time, the playwright's other work and biography, and the original production context - because an audience believes a world that is accurately furnished.

The play's architecture is then mapped: acts and scenes, entrances and exits, entrances that are announced and those that surprise, the rhythm of tension and release, the placement and length of climaxes, the tempo of each scene, and the turning points on which the action changes direction. Practitioners often build a beat sheet or a French scene breakdown (a new scene each time a character enters or exits) to see structure, and a character through-line for each role, tracing what the character wants, how it changes and where the decisive choices fall. Language is analysed for register - verse or prose, heightened or everyday, dialect or standard, formal or intimate - for imagery and motif, for shifts and interruptions, and for the silences and non-answers that are often the most significant lines in a scene. Staging implications are noted: why a writer has a character enter at that moment, why an object is specified, what a stage direction demands, and where the play's practical traps lie (scene changes, quick costume changes, animals, children, weather, water, fight sequences, size of cast).

Interpretation follows evidence: a director's concept is a reading of the play that makes coherent sense of its themes and world, and different productions of the same script may legitimately set it in another period or place, transpose it to a Caribbean setting, cross-gender or cross-race the casting, or place the emphasis on a different theme - provided the reading is supported by the text and communicated consistently through all the production choices. Concepts that contradict the text, ignore its structure or merely decorate it produce confusion, because the audience receives contradictory signals. The most valuable analytical habit is to state a proposition ('this play is about the price of loyalty in a small community'), then to test it against every scene: where is it supported, where is it challenged, and what does the ending do to it? A production built on a tested reading, delivered with accurate attention to the text, is convincing even with limited resources; a production with elaborate effects and no reading is not.
objectives: Gather textual evidence about given circumstances, character and language
Map the structure, beats, turning points and practical staging demands of a script
Form and justify an interpretive concept for a production

experiment.description: Concept Tester: Propose a production concept and test it against three scenes of the chosen play.

lessons.title: Playwriting, Devising and Caribbean Theatre Texts
lessons.content:
Playwriting begins with an idea that has dramatic potential - a situation containing conflict, or a character with an urgent want - rather than with a message. The writer decides whose story it is, what they want, what opposes them, and what change the action will force. Structure follows: the writer plans the plot, the sequence of scenes, the escalations and reversals, the climax and the ending, bearing in mind that a play must be performed in real time and that the audience can only know what they see and hear. Then comes the hard work of drafting and rewriting - writing the whole play through, reading it aloud, hearing it with actors, cutting, sharpening, and rewriting again, because a first draft is material rather than a finished play. Dialogue must be speakable and playable: short turns, interruptions, subtext, action carried in what is said and withheld, and distinct voices for each character. Formatting matters as craft: character names, stage directions in italics or brackets, setting and time stated at the head of each scene, and consistent layout so that actors, designers and stage managers can read and use the script.

Devising makes theatre without a pre-existing script, from a stimulus: an image, a photograph, a news story, a piece of music, a poem, a memory, a place, an object or a theme. The company researches the stimulus, improvises material around it, shapes and selects the strongest moments, records and structures them, adds text, movement, song, music, mask or design, and refines the whole in rehearsal until it runs. Improvisation is the working method: players accept each other's offers rather than blocking them, stay present, listen, play objectives and status, and allow scenes to develop; rehearsal techniques such as hot-seating, role-on-the-wall, freeze frames, thought tracking, cross-cutting and forum interventions generate and test material. Devised work suits Caribbean community, youth, issue-based and touring theatre, because it can be built from local experience and performed with few resources, and it produces scripts that belong to the performers who made them - which must be acknowledged and credited when the work is published or restaged.

Caribbean dramatic writing is one of the region's major literatures. Its landmarks include the folk-dialect and comedy traditions of the early twentieth century; the historical and poetic drama of Derek Walcott (whose work, including Dream on Monkey Mountain and Ti-Jean and His Brothers, brought Caribbean language and myth onto the international stage), the lyrical folk drama of Errol Hill and the pioneering Trinidad Theatre Workshop; Trevor Rhone's Jamaican plays of social comedy and its sharp satire of class and migration; Dennis Scott, Errol John, Lennox Brown, Una Marson, Sylvia Wynter, Zeno Obi Constance, Earl Lovelace, Mustapha Matura, Michael Anthony, Alwin Bully, Kendel Hippolyte, Grace Nichols and many others in poetry, theatre, pantomime and screen; and the continuing work of contemporary playwrights and companies staging new Caribbean work in the region and its diaspora. Studying these texts teaches the central lesson of playwriting: that the language an audience actually speaks - including its dialects, rhythms and humour - is a dramatic resource, not a limitation, and that the most effective dialogue on a Caribbean stage is the one that could be heard in the street outside it.
objectives: Draft, structure and rewrite a short scene or play with playable dialogue
Devise theatre from a stimulus using improvisation and rehearsal techniques
Discuss major Caribbean plays and playwrights and the use of dialect on stage

experiment.description: Devise Board: Turn a stimulus into scenes through improvisation and select what earns its place.

lessons.title: Elements of Dance and Rhythm
lessons.content:
Dance is organised movement, and it is analysed through a small set of elements. The body is the instrument: its parts, shapes, alignment, posture, and the difference between whole-body and isolated movement. Action describes what the body does - locomotion (travelling such as walking, running, skipping, sliding, rolling), non-locomotion (bending, twisting, stretching, gesturing, rising, falling), and stillness, which is itself a movement choice. Space concerns where the body moves: level (low, middle, high), direction, pathway (straight, curved, zigzag, spiral), size (large or small), shape (symmetrical or asymmetrical) and focus, and also the shape of the group on stage - lines, circles, diagonals, clusters, files and the formations that show relationships and shifts of power. Time concerns timing: tempo (fast, slow), rhythm (the pattern of beats), metre, duration, accent, syncopation, and the relationship of the dancer to the musical phrase - on the beat, ahead of it or delayed. Energy (sometimes called dynamics or effort) describes how the movement is performed: strong or light, sustained or sudden, bound or free, direct or indirect, and it conveys emotion more powerfully than the steps themselves. These elements together form the vocabulary of composition.

Rhythm, music and accompaniment are the dancer's partners. Caribbean performance is inseparable from its music - the drumming traditions of the region, the rhythms of mento, ska, rocksteady, reggae, dance hall, soca, calypso, cadence, kompa, reggaeton, merengue and bachata - and dancers learn to hear the clave, the bass, the break and the pulse, and to move with and against them. Dance may be performed to live or recorded music, to drumming, to song, to spoken word and narration, to body percussion and clapping, or in silence, and the choice changes the feeling of the work. Counting and cueing are practical skills: dancers count in eights, agree the beat on which an entrance or lift occurs, and follow the musical cues that hold a piece together when a recording is used.

Warm-up, conditioning and safety are inseparable from dance practice. Dancers warm up the whole body before working - mobilising joints, raising the heart rate, then dynamic stretching, before any static stretching - and cool down afterwards, and they train strength, flexibility, balance, stamina and alignment over months. Dance on hard floors in poor shoes or barefoot with a bad surface causes injury; a sprung, clean, non-slip floor is the professional requirement, as are safe shoes or bare feet according to the form, adequate space and sight of other dancers, water and rest, and prompt attention to pain, since overuse injuries to ankles, knees, hips and lower backs are common. Lifts and partner work need trained strength, agreed technique, spotting and rehearsal at reduced speed; jumps need landing technique with the knees soft and the weight controlled; and acrobatic or aerial elements require specialist coaching and supervision. Performance itself makes further demands - stamina, concentration, spacing and awareness of other performers, the ability to recover from errors without signalling them, and the projection of intention to the back of the house.
objectives: Analyse movement using body, action, space, time and energy
Relate dance to rhythm, music and accompaniment in Caribbean forms
Train, warm up, cool down and work safely, including in lifts and jumps

experiment.description: Movement Analyser: Describe a dance sequence using body, action, space, time and energy, then change one element.

lessons.title: Caribbean Dance Forms and Traditions
lessons.content:
The Caribbean's dance heritage is layered and living. Indigenous peoples danced ceremonially; African people brought to the region - through enslavement and later migration - traditions of sacred and social dance, drumming, ring games, procession and masquerade, which survived and adapted in the plantations, yards and villages. European country dances were taught in colonial households and absorbed into local practice; East Indian indentured workers brought their own dance and ritual forms, which continue in the region's Hindu and Muslim communities; and Chinese, Middle Eastern and other arrivals contributed further traditions. The result is a set of forms that are distinctively Caribbean and recognised abroad, from the quadrille and maypole to soca, dancehall and carnival mas.

The folk and traditional dances are the historical base. Quadrille - a set dance performed in figures by couples, to a caller and to live music, in the Jamaican, Trinidadian and other versions - shows the European figure-dance inheritance transformed by local rhythm and style. Maypole dancing, in which dancers weave ribbons around a pole in patterns, derives from spring and harvest celebrations and is still performed in schools and village festivals. Jonkonnu or John Canoe is a costumed Christmas masquerade with set characters - the House, the Cow Head, Pitchy Patchy, the Horse Head - and their own dances; Bruckins, a stately processional dance in period costume, commemorates emancipation; Dinki Mini, Gerreh, Kumina and Ettu carry African-derived ritual and social movement in Jamaica; the Bongo, Bélé, Kalinda, Limbo, Shango and Bele traditions belong to Trinidad and the wider region; Hosay processions, bhangra-influenced forms and tassa drumming belong to Indo-Caribbean communities; and Haitian Vodou dancing, Dominican merengue and bachata, Cuban rumba, son and mambo, and Puerto Rican bomba and plena each preserve distinct regional histories. Carnival masquerade adds its own vocabulary of character dances - Midnight Robber, Pierrot Grenade, Moko Jumbie on stilts, Jab Jab and the great bands of mas - while dancehall and soca carry contemporary social dance into the streets and the world.

Classical, contemporary and popular dance are equally part of the region's present. The National Dance Theatre Companies and schools of Jamaica, Trinidad, Cuba, Puerto Rico, Haiti and elsewhere train dancers in ballet, modern, Afro-Caribbean and contemporary techniques and produce original repertoire; choreographers such as Rex Nettleford (Jamaica) and Boscoe and Geoffrey Holder (Trinidad) brought Caribbean movement into theatre and to international stages; and contemporary companies work across dance, theatre, carnival and film. Studying these forms properly means researching rather than imitating: learning the origin, purpose, community and rules of each dance, working with practitioners and teachers from that tradition, using correct music and costume where the tradition requires it, and crediting the source when a form is adapted for the stage - because many of these dances are sacred, communal or contested, and take them out of context risks disrespect even when the movement is copied accurately.
objectives: Describe Caribbean folk and traditional dance forms and their cultural origins
Explain contemporary, classical and popular dance practice in the region

lessons.title: Choreography, Composition and Staging Dance
lessons.content:
Choreography is the art of making dances, and it follows an intentional process. It begins with the choreographer's intent: what the dance is for, what it should communicate or make the audience feel, whether it is narrative (telling a story), thematic (exploring an idea or emotion), abstract (exploring movement itself) or functional (a character dance, a ritual or a production number within a play). Research follows - the music, the cultural form, the period, the visual references, the movement vocabulary that fits - and then exploration begins with improvisation to tasks: move only on the floor, move as if the space is shrinking, make a phrase from three gestures, dance the feeling of this line of text. The choreographer records ideas on video, writes them in movement notation or spoken counts, and keeps only what works, which is a process of selection as much as invention.

Composition builds phrases and structures from the selected material. A motif - a short, memorable movement phrase - is developed by varying what is done with it: change the level, the tempo, the direction, the energy, the size, the number of dancers, the relationship between dancers, or repeat it with one element altered. Unison, canon, contrast, counterpoint, accumulation and chance sequencing are standard devices, and the stage picture is composed deliberately with formations - lines, circles, diagonals, clusters, files, entrances and exits - that carry meaning and keep the audience's eye moving. Structure is planned in sections, with transitions between them, at least one clear climax and a resolution, and with attention to how long the audience can hold attention before a change is needed. Musicality, spacing, sight lines, costume movement, floor surface and the amount of rehearsal available all shape the final composition: an ambitious lift fails on an unlit stage with a wet floor, and a beautiful phrase performed twice as fast as rehearsed reads as panic.

Staging dance brings it in front of an audience. Rehearsals are scheduled around the dancers' availability, technical needs and the physical demands of the material, with warm-ups, water and rest built in and the riskiest passages rehearsed early and often; a stage manager or rehearsal director keeps the notes and the running order. Lighting and costume are designed for movement, not portraits: lighting that leaves the face in shadow but throws the body into relief, side and back light to define shape, colour that survives the light, costumes that allow the required range and do not slip, catch or shed, footwear that grips, and a floor that does not injure. The performance is then run and re-run: dancers learn to enter and exit on cue, to maintain spacing and formations, to recover from mistakes without signalling them, and to project the intention of the piece through the whole body to the last row. After the performance the choreographer evaluates honestly - what the audience saw, what the dancers felt, where the piece sagged - and records it, since a dance that is not documented survives only in the memories of those who danced it.
objectives: Devise a movement motif and develop it through variation
Compose and structure a dance with formations, transitions and a clear climax
Rehearse, light, costume and stage a dance piece safely and evaluate the performance

experiment.description: Choreo Loop: Build a motif, apply five variations and assemble them into a structured phrase.

lessons.title: Set Design, Props and Stage Technology
lessons.content:
Set design creates the world of the play and answers the practical needs of the action. It begins with reading the script for its demands - the places required, the doors and windows that must open, stairs, levels, entrances and exits, the furniture the action uses, the items that must be concealed or revealed - and continues with research into the period, place and social world of the play, visual sources and reference photographs, and discussion with the director about concept and style. From that comes the design: a ground plan showing every piece of furniture and scenery in position from above, drawn to scale on gridded paper; elevations showing the vertical design of the walls and flats; a model box, a scale model of the set in a box open on the audience side, which shows volume, colour and proportion better than any drawing; a materials and colour schedule; and a props list divided into furniture, set dressing (the small items that make a space look inhabited) and hand props (used by the actors).

Construction and stage technology turn design into reality. Sets may be built from timber frames covered with canvas or hardboard, from flats joined, braced and weighted so that they stand, from rostra and platforms at different levels, from permanently built stock pieces, or from found and improvised materials - the resourceful Caribbean approach of using what is available, from bamboo and boxes to rented scaffolding. Practical scenery must meet the demands of performance: doors that close, windows that open, a table that holds real weight, furniture that does not wobble, pieces that can be moved silently in the dark during a scene change, and masking that hides the wings. Scenery is usually painted and textured ('flatted') to look like its material under stage light rather than daylight, because stage light flattens and colours shift. Rigging and flying, revolves, trucks, trapdoors and automation add movement but multiply risk; safe practice requires load limits, correct hardware, inspection and, for anything complex, qualified riggers and operators.

Health and safety governs everything built and handled on stage. Scenery must be stable, weighted and secured so nothing can topple on a performer; platforms need solid construction, edge markings and handrails where height or fall risk exists; stairs need consistent rise and visible edges; tools used in construction - saws, drills, staplers, paint and solvents - require safe technique, protective equipment, ventilation and careful housekeeping with cables taped down and offcuts cleared; paint and solvents are stored safely and no smoking or flame is allowed near them; heavy pieces are moved with trolleys and two people and not with the back; and the stage is inspected before every performance for loose screws, wobbling furniture and obstacles in the dark. Props have their own rules: food and drink props must be safe to consume, glass is replaced with plastic wherever it can break, weapons and anything resembling a weapon are logged, checked and stored securely with the weapon master, and pyrotechnics, flame, smoke and water effects are only used with specialist training, permissions and a written risk assessment. A set that looks magnificent and hurts someone is a failed design.
objectives: Read a script for design requirements and research the world of the play
Produce a ground plan, elevations, model box and props list for a chosen scene
Identify construction, rigging and stage safety requirements and controls

experiment.description: Set Planner: Turn a scene's requirements into a ground plan and check every entrance, level and prop.

lessons.title: Costume, Make-up, Hair and Mask
lessons.content:
Costume design does three jobs at once: it tells the audience who a character is, it supports the actor's performance, and it serves the practical demands of the production. The designer reads the script for time, place, season, social class, occupation, age, wealth and the character's own attitude to dress, then researches sources - paintings, photographs, museum garments, family albums, interviews, market and fabric shops - before sketching ideas and presenting them. A costume plot lists every character and every change, with the scene, and shows which changes are quick and which require help, because a costume that cannot be changed in ninety seconds backstage will wreck the show even if it is beautiful. Practical criteria then govern: fit and mobility for the actor's movement, durability across a run, laundering and repair, safety (no tripping hems, restricting sleeves, loose jewellery or flammable synthetics near open flame), colour that survives stage lighting, the budget, the availability of fabric and makers, and fitting the available dressing rooms, racks and quick-change space.

Make-up and hair complete the character and are planned in the same way. Straight make-up corrects and enhances so the face reads under stage light, which exaggerates shadows and washes out colour; character make-up ages, creates illness or injury, alters features or creates animal and fantasy looks; and special effects include burns, scars, wounds, tattoos, beards and bald caps, built with greasepaint, cream, powder, latex, wax, spirit gum, hair and prosthetics. Hygiene is non-negotiable: each performer has their own applicators and sponges where possible, shared items are disinfected, products are not exchanged between faces, allergy tests are done for adhesives and colours, performers remove make-up properly afterwards, and eyes and skin are respected. Period and cultural hairstyles, wigs, braids and cornrows, headwraps and adornment must be researched and, where a cultural practice is depicted, done with understanding rather than costume-shop caricature. Performers must also be consulted and treated with dignity: make-up and hair are performed on a person, and consent, comfort and privacy matter.

Masks are a distinct design discipline that shapes performance as well as appearance. A mask covers the face, so meaning must be carried by the body, which is why masked work is physical, large and precise; the mask's character exists only when it is animated by movement, and the actor must decide where the mask's attention is directed rather than actually looking with their own eyes. Masks may be full or half, rigid (paper mache, leather, wood, plastic, resin), soft fabric or wire, comic, grotesque, ceremonial or neutral; they may be built from a life cast of the performer's face, or from clay, plaster, cardboard, papier mache or light foam, decorated and finished with elastic, ties or a head harness. Carnival and mas traditions are the region's great mask and costume laboratory, and mas builders are among its most skilled designers. Costume and mask construction also carries hazards - hot glue, spray adhesives, aerosol paint, cutting tools, feathers and dust, and airborne particles - and safe practice is the same as in any workshop: ventilation, masks, gloves, sharp safe tools, and careful storage.
objectives: Design a costume plot with practical criteria for fit, change, durability and safety
Plan and apply stage make-up and hair hygienically and with respect for the performer
Explain mask design and construction and its effect on how the actor performs

experiment.description: Costume Call: Build a costume plot with the changes and check for the quick changes that will fail backstage.

lessons.title: Lighting, Sound and Stage Management
lessons.content:
Lighting makes the audience see, feel and believe. Its functions are visibility (the audience must see faces and action where and when it matters), focus (concentrating the eye on the acting area or isolating a character), mood and time of day and place (warm and bright for a morning, cold and low for night, dappled and green for a forest), atmosphere and style (realistic or atmospheric, harsh or soft), and composition (lighting the stage picture, creating shadow and highlighting shape). Lighting is planned in a plot - a plan of the theatre showing the position of every instrument and its circuit or address - a gel or colour list, a focus session in which each instrument is aimed, and a cue sheet that records each cue's number, the moment it is called, its fade time and the state it produces. The basic instruments include profile spots with shutters and gobo slots for definition and texture, fresnels for soft wash, par cans and LED fixtures for colour and effects, follow spots for soloists and practical sources such as lamps, candles or a fire effect for realism. Colour is chosen for the pink, amber, straw, blue and green range used on stage, remembering that coloured light mixes differently from paint and that gel fades, burns and must be checked before the run.

Sound design covers everything the audience hears: music (live or recorded, and how it is performed or played), effects (doors, phone, weather, traffic, animals, gunshots, ambience), reinforcement of voices so that they are audible in a large or awkward space, and the mix between them. It is planned as a sound plot and a cue sheet, with sources (laptop, phone, mixer, playback software, CD, live musicians and singers), speakers and their placement, radio microphones and their checking, and the levels at which voices are comfortable and effects are effective without being painful. Sound cues are almost always the hardest to run 'by eye', so a cue is given a clear call point - a line, an action, a lighting cue - and the operator rehearses it in the technical rehearsal until it is repeatable. Both lighting and sound are also governed by safety: correct and unleaded cabling run so that nobody trips, no unauthorised access to lanterns or rigging, no dark stage without a plan for safe movement, sound levels that respect hearing, and battery management for radio microphones.

Stage management is the discipline that holds the production together. The stage manager prepares the rehearsal room, keeps the prompt book with script, blocking notes, props list, running order, cue sheets and contact details, makes the rehearsal diary and calls the company, takes rehearsal notes and distributes them, arranges the props and the set, and, once the show runs, calls every cue so that lighting, sound, fly and scene-change operate together in the right order. Cue calls are made in standard language - warning, standby and go - over a comms system or by a clearly agreed signal. The stage manager also manages the performers backstage: calls for entrances (the half-hour, the fifteen, the five, beginners), the sign-in, costume and make-up timing, silent scene changes, keeping the wings clear and lit safely, and handling the unexpected - an illness, a missing prop, a late audience. Front-of-house staff work with the stage manager to hold the performance until the audience is ready and the actors are in position and to hold or delay a start when something is wrong. After each performance the stage manager writes a performance report: timings, audience numbers, technical problems, injuries, audience reaction - the record that makes the next performance and the next production better.
objectives: Design a lighting plan and cue sheet for a scene and explain its effects
Plan sound sources, reinforcement and cues, and check levels and safety
Carry out stage management duties: prompt book, calls, cue calling and performance reports

experiment.description: Cue Caller: Write a cue sheet and call a sequence of lighting and sound cues in the right order.

lessons.title: From Rehearsal to Performance
lessons.content:
A production moves through a defined sequence, and each stage has its own work. Planning and auditioning come first: the script is chosen and rights obtained, a budget agreed, the production team and schedules set, auditions run with prepared readings, improvisation or workshop exercises and callbacks, and the cast announced with the first rehearsal date. Then the rehearsal period: a read-through and design presentation, blocking and working rehearsals for each scene, character and business, off-book deadlines, then run-throughs of acts and the whole play to find pace, continuity and energy. Design and build run in parallel from the first week - sets built and painted, costumes made and fitted, props found or made, lights plotted and focused, sound recorded and edited, poster, programme, tickets and publicity produced - and production meetings keep the timelines and budgets visible. Props and costume rehearsals matter as much as line rehearsals, because an actor handling a real object for the first time on the first night will be slow, cautious and visibly acting.

The technical and dress rehearsals integrate everything. Technical rehearsals ('tech') work through the show cue by cue with the actors in position, often in costume but not full performance, adjusting levels, timings, scene changes and sight lines and recording every cue; a cue-to-cue may be run first for the complex sequences; the dress rehearsal runs the whole production at performance pace, in costume, make-up and full technical state, and is the last chance to find the problems - a slow quick change, a dark entrance, a microphone that fails, a scene change that takes too long in the blackout. Notes are given after each rehearsal, from the director to the actors and from the stage manager to the technical team, written and specific rather than general. A preview performance may be given to an audience before the official opening, precisely so that an audience's presence - their laughter, silences, attention and restlessness - can be learned and adjusted to.

Performance discipline keeps a run consistent and safe. Performers arrive in good time, sign in, warm up the voice and body, apply make-up and costume, check props and quick changes, and are at their places for the beginners call; they maintain concentration, energy and character for the whole performance, whatever the audience does, and do not break character, comment on mistakes or improvise into another actor's scene without agreement. Front of house opens at the right time, seats the audience and manages latecomers, safety announcements and evacuations; the stage manager calls the show and supervises the backstage; the technical operators stay alert through their quiet periods; and the producer watches over the audiences, income and any incidents. After the run comes the strike - dismantling the set, returning borrowed items, cleaning and storing costumes, props and equipment, settling accounts and thanking everyone - followed by an evaluation meeting: what worked, what did not, what the audience response and any reviews said, and what the company will do differently next time. Companies that evaluate honestly improve; companies that do not repeat the same disaster annually.
objectives: Describe the production process from auditions through technical and dress rehearsals
Prepare for and maintain performance discipline through a run
Carry out strike, evaluation and company administration after a production

experiment.description: Production Timeline: Lay out a production schedule from audition to strike and find the impossible weeks.

lessons.title: Appreciation, Criticism and Audience
lessons.content:
Appreciation is the disciplined enjoyment and understanding of a performance, and it can be learned. It begins with attention: watching the whole event, noticing what is on stage and what is happening in the audience, and resisting the urge to decide before the play is over. The performance event itself includes everything - the space and how the audience is arranged, the programme, the pre-show and interval, the atmosphere, the seating, the temperature, the audience's response - all of which are part of what the production means. After the performance, the appreciative spectator separates their impressions: what they saw (the production choices - casting, design, staging, pace, style), what they felt and when (the moments that moved, amused, bored or confused them), and why (the specific choices responsible). This is the opposite of the two commonest responses - 'I liked it' and 'I didn't understand it' - because it names the evidence on which taste rests.

Criticism is the written or spoken expression of that analysis, and it has a professional tradition with real responsibilities. A review describes what the production did, interprets it in relation to the play and the production's concept, evaluates how well it worked against its own intentions and the audience's experience, and does so with evidence, specific examples and fair judgement. It should be written for a reader who may not have seen the show: naming the play, playwright, company, venue and dates, praising and faulting precisely, avoiding personal attack, and being aware of the difference between a production that failed and one that was not to the reviewer's taste. A review is also contextual: it may consider the production's place in a community's life, its cultural and historical context, its budget and circumstances, and its contribution to the region's theatre. Students of theatre write reviews to learn to see, and the discipline of finding exact words for a lighting choice or a moment of acting is one of the best exercises in the subject.

The audience is a live participant, not a passive receiver. It affects the performance directly: laughter pushes comedy, attentive silence holds tragedy, and a restive house flattens energy; actors adjust pace and timing to the responses they get, and stage managers hold the start until the audience is seated. Audiences also bring expectations, knowledge and culture, and a single production may be received quite differently by different groups - a school matinee, a festival crowd, a community audience, a diaspora audience, critics, elders and young people. Audience research uses questionnaires, interviews, box-office data, talkbacks and social media to find out who came, what they thought and whether they would return, and this information drives programming, marketing and pricing decisions. Theatre etiquette is the practical expression of this relationship: arriving on time and having phones silenced, not talking or filming during the performance, not eating noisily, applauding appropriately, respecting the performers and the people around you, and, in participatory Caribbean forms where audience response is invited, taking part with energy. Learning to be a good audience is part of learning theatre.
objectives: Analyse a performance's choices, effects and meanings with specific evidence
Write a balanced, informative review of a live performance
Explain the audience's role, audience research methods and theatre etiquette

experiment.description: Review Draft: Watch a described scene, separate what you saw from what you felt, and write the review paragraph.

lessons.title: Caribbean Theatre, Arts Enterprise and Safe Practice
lessons.content:
Caribbean theatre has a continuous history and a living present. Its strands include the folk and festival performance traditions - Carnival and calypso theatre, Jonkonnu, Junkanoo, Hosay, Maypole, ring games, storytelling and Christmas sports - which are participatory, outdoor and community-owned; the colonial-era amateur and school theatricals; and, in the twentieth century, the emergence of a professional and literary theatre, with the Trinidad Theatre Workshop and the pioneering work of Derek Walcott and Errol Hill, the Jamaican pantomime and its dialect comedy, Trevor Rhone and the Jamaican stage, national theatre companies, the Little Theatre Movement and its annual pantomime, national dance theatre companies in Jamaica, Trinidad, Cuba and elsewhere, community and street theatre, festival and carnival arts, the Schools' Drama Festival and national drama festivals, and the regional CARIFESTA gatherings that bring the region's companies together. Contemporary theatre works in traditional venues, black boxes, schools, churches, yards, buses, beaches, heritage sites and online, and combines drama with dance, music, spoken word, comedy, mas and digital design - the region's theatre is characterised by musicality, humour, direct address, political edge and the central place of language.

Theatre is also work, and it increasingly organises itself as enterprise. Careers include acting, directing, writing and dramaturgy, choreography, design (set, costume, lighting, sound, make-up), stage and production management, technical operation, arts administration, producing, marketing and front-of-house, teaching and community facilitation, broadcasting, film and voice work, festivals and events, carnival and mas production, costume and prop making, and the specialist trades of carpentry, welding, upholstery, wigmaking and tailoring that serve the industry. Most practitioners work project-to-project across several of these, so the practical disciplines of the freelance artist matter as much as talent: keeping a curriculum vitae and portfolio of work, photographs and reviews; auditioning well and preparing properly; costing your time and expenses and negotiating fees; writing and keeping written contracts, receipts and invoices; registering and paying taxes and social contributions as required; budgeting a production and preparing funding applications to arts councils, sponsors, ministries and development agencies; protecting your intellectual property and obtaining performance rights before staging someone else's script; marketing work through social media, photography, trailers and press; building professional relationships and referring work to others; managing the irregular income of a creative career; and looking after health, voice and body across years of work.

Safety is a professional obligation throughout, and every participant shares it. The theatre has real hazards: rigging, working at height, counterweight systems, power tools and construction, electrical work and cabling, the heat of lanterns, the water and slippery surfaces of some effects, the noise levels of music and effects, pyrotechnics, flame, weapons and fight sequences, trip hazards and darkness backstage, crowd density in foyers, and the physical demands of lifting, dancing and long technical rehearsals. Controls are practical: proper induction and training before persons are asked to do hazardous work, licensed and competent specialists for electrical and rigging tasks, correct equipment used within limits, protective clothing and footwear, hearing protection, clear and lit walkways, taped cables, fire extinguishers and exits kept clear, rehearsed evacuation plans, first aid provision and an accident book, food, water and rest breaks in long rehearsal periods, and a written risk assessment for anything unusual - fire, smoke, water, heights, animals, children and weapons. Every company also needs its policies on working with minors, on harassment and bullying, on inclusivity and access, and on respect for cultural and personal dignity in casting, costume and content - because a theatre cannot claim to speak for a community while treating any of its members badly. The region's theatre has been built by people who took the art seriously and each other seriously; that combination is what you are being trained to continue.
objectives: Describe Caribbean theatre traditions, institutions and contemporary practice
Explain the careers and business skills required to work professionally in theatre
Apply health, safety, ethical and inclusion practice in rehearsal and production

experiment.description: Career Planner: Map a route through the theatre industry, cost a first year and identify the training each role needs.
